section.title: Final projects
section.p: The book began with two instruments on a dashboard. One measured accumulated distance. The other measured instantaneous change.
Since then, the same two ideas have appeared in many forms:
section.md: \text{derivatives measure local change}, \qquad \text{integrals accumulate small pieces}.
section.p: Taylor polynomials turned local derivative information into approximations. Differential equations turned laws of change into unknown functions. Parametric curves let motion draw geometry. Fourier ideas built periodic motion from waves. The one-dimensional Stokes theorem revealed the Fundamental Theorem as a boundary theorem.
These final projects ask you to use the whole story.

figure.caption: Calculus is one connected language: change, accumulation, approximation, models, and boundary terms.

section.p: Each project below can be done alone or with a small group. A good solution should include clear calculations, graphs when they help, and a short written explanation of what the calculations mean.

subsection.title: Model, solve, and test a cooling law
subsection.p: Newton’s law of cooling was one of our first differential equation models:
It says that the rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference between the object and its surroundings.
This project asks you to build the model from data, solve it, and then test whether it deserves to be trusted.

exercise.title: Why must a model be solved and then tested?

statement.p: The cooling project asks you to solve Newton’s law, estimate a constant from data, and then check whether the model deserves trust. In your own words, why is solving a differential equation not the end of the scientific story, and what does a mismatch with data force you to admit?

hint.p: A solved formula is only as good as the law and the measurements that produced it. Testing asks whether the local rule actually shapes the observed global behavior.

exercise.title: Why is an approximation incomplete without an error bound?

statement.p: The integral and Taylor-calculator projects compare several numerical methods and insist on a stopping rule. In your own words, why can three different approximations of the same integral still be unfinished work until their errors are controlled?

hint.p: More digits are not a guarantee. An error bound turns a computation into a promise, which is the same remainder idea that made Taylor series into algorithms.

subsection.title: Build a Taylor-series calculator
subsection.p: A calculator evaluates functions so quickly that it is easy to forget the question:
subsection.md: \text{How does the calculator know the value?}
subsection.p: For many functions, one answer is Taylor series. The calculator does not store every value of \sin x, e^x, or \cos x. It uses algorithms, and Taylor polynomials are one of the first algorithms we can understand.

paragraphs.title: Warning: small terms are not always enough
paragraphs.p: A common mistake is to stop when the next term is small, without knowing whether the tail is controlled. For alternating series with decreasing terms, that is justified. For other series, it may not be.
A calculator must be fast, but it must also be honest.

subsection.p: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says
For most of the book, this was the theorem that connected antiderivatives and definite integrals. In Section , we gave it a second meaning:
The derivative is accumulated over the interval. The original function is evaluated on the boundary.

paragraphs.p: The exact higher-dimensional theorems belong to multivariable calculus. But the pattern already appears in one dimension:

exercise.title: Why is the Fundamental Theorem the first boundary theorem?

statement.p: One project asks you to explain the FTC as a telescoping finite-difference statement that becomes an integral of a derivative. In your own words, why do interior cancellations leave only the boundary, and why does that viewpoint point toward Green, Stokes, and the Divergence Theorem?

hint.p: Adding consecutive changes cancels everything except the last value minus the first. In higher dimensions the same pattern remains: what happens inside is measured by what happens on the oriented boundary.

subsection.title: Closing note: what calculus has taught us
subsection.p: This book has followed one thread through many forms.
A derivative began as a velocity:
Then it became a tangent slope, a local linear approximation, a sensitivity, an optimizer, and a law of change.
An integral began as accumulated distance:
Then it became area, mass, work, probability, numerical approximation, and a boundary principle.
A Taylor polynomial began as a local approximation:
Then it became a gateway to infinite series, Euler’s formula, and waves.
The same ideas now point outward.

subsection.p: The subject is larger than this book. But the central pattern is already here:
subsection.md: \text{calculus measures change, accumulates change, and explains how local rules shape global behavior.}
subsection.p: That pattern is worth carrying forward.

exercise.title: What pattern has calculus been teaching all along?

statement.p: The book began with a speedometer and an odometer and ended with series, waves, conservation, and paths. In your own words, why are derivatives, integrals, remainders, and boundary terms one language rather than four subjects, and what does it mean that local rules shape global behavior?

hint.p: Instantaneous change and accumulated change undo each other. Approximations become trustworthy through error. Models and conservation laws turn a local derivative statement into a global picture. That is the pattern to carry forward.
